reasons: Gaia radial velocity shows a stellar-mass companion: gaia_rv_variable True, gaia_rv_nb_transits 22, gaia_rv_renormalised_gof 71.2, gaia_rv_chisq_pvalue 0.0, gaia_rv_epoch_scatter_km_s 24.6, gaia_rv_amplitude_robust_km_s 76.9. A scatter of tens of km/s cannot come from a planet; step 9 itself bounds the companion at this period by gaia_rv_companion_mass_upper_limit_solar_masses 0.533, i.e. an M-dwarf-mass companion is allowed and a planet is not what the RV scatter implies. gaia_ruwe 1.48 (caution 'RUWE above 1.4') is consistent with the same companion.

The transit is grazing, so the photometric radius is unconstrained rather than a measured 36 Earth radii: fit_impact_parameter 1.179 +/- 0.1704, fit_radius_ratio 0.2317 +/- 0.15824, planet_radius_earth_radii 35.98 +/- 24.57, caution 'transit fit not converged in 100000 steps'. The record shows the fit flipping between b 0.45-0.48 with Rp ~5 Earth radii but density ratio 19.9-21.7 (runs 9674c6b, c651077) and b 1.18 with Rp 36 and density ratio 0.645 (runs a0cf3d7, 7983853). Either the duration does not fit the star (step 7 caution, fitted_to_expected_scaled_semi_major_axis 3.66, duration_hours 1.44 / fit_duration_hours 2.311 at period 11.53 d around stellar_radius_solar_radii 1.4258) or the transit is grazing. Both outcomes mean the light curve cannot say the companion is planet-sized, so the companion's nature must come from the RV, and the RV says stellar.

I partly disagree with the mechanical reasoning: 'radius 36.0 Earth radii above 22.4' is not by itself decisive because the grazing geometry leaves the radius almost unconstrained. The drop rests instead on the combination of a grazing, short-duration dip with the Gaia RV scatter, which together point to a grazing eclipsing binary; the conclusion is the same.

TRICERATOPS does not support a planet despite the verdict label: fpp_mean 0.4075 +/- 0.021 is far above any validation threshold and means the false-positive scenarios are nearly as likely as the planet scenario; nfpp_mean 0 and nearby_scenarios_excluded True only rule out the neighbours (Gaia DR3 3288837740527400576 at 23" and 3288834789885910784 at 51" from gaia_neighbours_able_to_cause_dip), so the remaining 41% is on-target companion scenarios, which is exactly what the RV indicates.

Secondary eclipse is marginal but in the EB direction: secondary_depth_ppm 166 +/- 63 (2.6 sigma) against secondary_maximum_planet_depth_ppm 287. Not a refutation on its own, but it does not help the planet case. ellipsoidal_amplitude_ppm -41 +/- 79 is uninformative at a/R 13.83 (fit_scaled_semi_major_axis).

The dip is real and on the target (pixel_verdict 'on target', S98 SNR 6.3, best star TIC 450075592; odd_even_difference_sigma 0.33), so this is not a blend or false alarm; it is a real eclipse of TIC 450075592, most likely by a stellar companion.

Sector 5 adds nothing and does not change the call: other_sector_results 'S5 TESS-SPOC: SNR 4.0, expected SNR 8.6', joint_search_snr 12.9 equals the S98-only MES 12.60321/BLS SNR 12.9, and the figure shows S5 data only at -32 to -24 h from the propagated mid-transit, so the 'depths differ between sectors' caution (cutout S5 r2.0 -113 +/- 140 vs S98 r2.0 1205 +/- 125, cutout_sector_depth_consistency_p_value 2.55e-12) reflects ephemeris propagation over ~217 cycles with fit_period_error_days 0.00118741 rather than a genuine depth change. I give it no weight either way.

Not 'held': released_tess_sectors_not_in_all_sector_verification is empty, and more TESS photometry would not remove the Gaia RV evidence; only ground-based RVs could, and those are outside this pipeline. exofop_tois, exofop_ctois and published_signal are empty, so the signal is new, but the evidence makes it most likely a stellar companion rather than a planet.
